newsitem.title: UK: EIB set to raise bulk of funds in euros from 1999.
newsitem.headline: EIB set to raise bulk of funds in euros from 1999.

text.p: The European Investment Bank plans to raise the bulk of its funds in the new euro currency in an effort to establish itself as the best credit available in euro-denominated bonds in 1999, an EIB executive said on Friday.

"We want to be the best credit and best distributor of euro bonds in Europe, the U.S. and Asia as a non-governmental institution alongside sovereigns," Rene Karsenti, director general of finance at the EIB, told a conference here.
"This is modest, simple, and we have the means to achieve that position," he said.
The triple A-rated EIB, the world's biggest borrower, currently has funding requirements exceeding 18 billion Ecu per year and Karsenti said this total was set to rise.
"The bulk of our issuance will be in the new euromarket as our debt will have features closer to government bonds, like auctions and primary dealers," Karsenti said.

"We will continue to use other markets for smaller, more tailor-made issuance and will also tap retail through offshore deals, but the bulk of funding will come from the new domestic European market," he said.
Karsenti said the move to a single currency, scheduled for 1999, would increase the importance of credit valuation since currency differences would vanish.

"Following EMU, national governments effectively become local governments...and credit valuation could become important, especially if a member state starts to encounter post-EMU structural problems," Karsenti said.
He said competition between governments to raise debt would be intense, with "liquidity and credit becoming the key factors in relative pricing".
A European corporate bond market might finally take off with EMU bringing better liquidity as more bonds for a given issuer are traded in the same currency.
The EIB has already started its strategy of establishing itself as a premier European credit.
"We are preparing ourselves for EMU and the current funding strategy reflects this. We have been issuing major benchmarks in key European markets," Karsenti said.
The EIB pays little over government paper in the international bond markets.

For example, it set a six billion French franc eight-year bond earlier this month at one basis point over French government paper. A 300 million stg deal maturing in 2003 was priced at only three b.p. over gilts.
